planting.note: Move outdoors or into bright conditions only after nights stay reliably above 50F, since this East African stem succulent has no frost tolerance.

directions: This clump-forming stapeliad produces slender, segmented, cactus-like stems that branch low from the base, gradually forming a dense mound. Small bell- or star-shaped flowers appear along the stem ridges in warm months, typically pale with fine maroon speckling. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining mineral mix and water only when the stem segments begin to look slightly deflated, withholding water almost entirely in winter. Native to arid stony ground in the Horn of Africa region, it is intolerant of overwatering and prefers bright, filtered light over intense direct midday sun in very hot climates.
sources: Bruyns, P.V., Stapeliads of Southern Africa and Madagascar

planting.note: Wait until well after last frost and overnight lows stabilize warm, since this slow-growing pebble-mimicry succulent resents any chill or damp cold.

directions: A highly sought 'living rock' stapeliad from the stony limestone terrain of northern Somalia, forming a rounded, tuberculate, pebble-like body that mimics the surrounding gravel. Small dark flowers with a fetid scent emerge near the crown in the growing season, typical of fly-pollinated stapeliads. It requires an extremely mineral, almost soil-free substrate with sharp drainage and should be watered sparingly, only in the warmest months, with a long dry rest otherwise. Because mature plants are rarely collected and seed-grown stock is scarce, it remains a prized specialist item among caudiciform and stapeliad collectors.
sources: Bruyns, P.V., Stapeliads of Southern Africa and Madagascar

planting.note: Start the tuber into growth after last frost once soil has warmed, as new shoots emerge quickly once temperatures rise in spring.

directions: This South African caudiciform grows from a swollen underground tuber, sending up thin twining or sprawling annual stems each season that die back completely at the end of the growing cycle. Clusters of maroon, star-shaped flowers with recurved, finely textured petal lobes appear along the stems in summer and have a faint carrion-like scent typical of the milkweed family. Keep the tuber nearly dry and undisturbed through its dormant season, resuming watering only once new growth is visible, and use a very porous mineral soil to prevent rot. It is a long-lived collector plant that slowly increases tuber size over many seasons of seasonal top growth and dormancy.
sources: Dyer, R.A., Asclepiadaceae treatments of southern African Brachystelma species

planting.note: Begin watering the tuber after last frost once warm weather settles in, since growth starts slowly and is easily stalled by cold, wet soil.

directions: A South African member of the milkweed family that forms a large partially exposed woody caudex below ground, from which thin twining vines emerge each growing season to scramble over neighboring plants or a support. Pale, waxy, star-shaped flowers appear in loose clusters along the vines during the warm months. The caudex should be kept completely dry through its winter dormancy and only lightly watered once active growth resumes, as it is highly prone to rot in cool, damp conditions. Collectors value it for the slowly thickening above-ground caudex, which can take many years to develop pronounced sculptural character.
sources: Dyer, R.A., The Genus Raphionacme in southern Africa

planting.note: Move into full light and resume regular watering after last frost, as this Madagascar native needs sustained warmth to stay in active growth.

directions: Endemic to dry forest and scrub in Madagascar, this dwarf stapeliad forms low, clustering clumps of slender, four-angled stems that spread slowly by offsets at the base. Small, intricately patterned flowers with fringed or textured petal surfaces appear near the stem tips, following the fly-pollination strategy common to the stapeliad tribe. It needs a very free-draining mineral mix, protection from prolonged damp or cold, and a reduced watering schedule during its cooler-season rest. Because habitat collection pressure and limited seed availability make it uncommon, most plants in cultivation come from small specialist stapeliad and caudiciform seed suppliers.
sources: Bruyns, P.V., Stapeliads of Southern Africa and Madagascar
